title: The Merchant of Jerusalem: the market that crossed a border
text: Dust hung thick over the stone market plaza, settling across baskets, awnings, and rooftops that had not shifted in generations... Voices called out prices in the same tones they always had, children darted between stalls, and the smell of spice and bread drifted along alleys that had never known a checkpoint. For generations, urban traders ran their stone market stalls on the very same corners, selling to the very same families, trading gossip and goods across narrow aisles that had witnessed weddings, funerals, arguments, and ordinary Tuesdays alike, all without a single new line drawn through their center. But riders of geopolitical change suddenly shifted the city lines during the escalations of 1967, and the market plaza that had always felt whole woke up one morning divided. Some buyers stepped into the familiar stalls, looked around at faces they didn't recognize, and stepped right back out again, asking quietly where the original shopkeepers had gone... as though the stones themselves had rearranged overnight while everyone slept. So local merchants adjusted their trades, learning new customers, new delivery routes, new unspoken rules about who could sell where and when. But the sudden administrative division of Jerusalem meant about 1.5 million ordinary residents faced immediate, daily changes in how they crossed their own city simply to reach work each morning, school each afternoon, or family each evening. So municipal authorities pushed for heavy, permanent infrastructure, checkpoints and barriers rising where open alleys and footpaths once stood freely. And it took more than 50 years from the initial conflict before these internal dividing lines began to feel normal, even invisible, to the younger generations who had never once known the market plaza any other way than divided.
